headline: High: shared browser/network and file-handling surfaces create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks; B is safer on writes but still inherits A’s unverified outputs.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can run browsers, use broad network egress, and inject runtime MCPs/hooks; agent B is a CLI social uploader that can consume external content and account data. A shared or copied content path is plausible, but no direct shared channel is documented, so I choose medium rather than low because A’s browser-facing ingestion can carry attacker-controlled text into B.
conditions: IF A ingests untrusted web content and forwards it into B’s upload inputs, injection becomes actionable.
IF the operator copies A-generated text into B without review, prompt injection can propagate.
mitigations: Require manual review of any A-produced text before B uses it.
Disable browser-driven content ingestion for A when preparing B uploads.
Use a fixed template for B captions/descriptions.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags from A to B inputs.
requires-engineering: isolate A and B into separate workspaces.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches session history, project code, AGENTS.md, README.md, and provider auth data; B touches video, images, and account data. Even though B cannot read files by profile, A’s broad egress and browser use make accidental transfer of sensitive material into B’s outbound uploads plausible in default workflows, so the pair presents a medium leakage risk.
conditions: IF A’s session history or provider auth data is copied into B inputs, leakage occurs.
IF B uploads media that contains secrets or internal code from A’s workspace, exfiltration occurs.
mitigations: Review media and captions for secrets before B uploads.
Keep A’s auth prompts and session history in a separate profile.
Use a redaction checklist for filenames, overlays, and screenshots.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace separation between A and B.
requires-engineering: add content scanning before B uploads.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has broad network and subprocess capability, while B explicitly cannot write the filesystem, modify git state, or execute shells. That makes direct write-write conflict unlikely; the main overlap is read/use of shared external services, so the conflict surface is limited and low severity.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mutable external account or API quota, contention can occur.
IF an orchestrator grants B additional write permissions, conflict severity increases.
mitigations: Keep B on read-only inputs except for its upload API.
Avoid running both agents against the same mutable account simultaneously.
Stagger jobs to prevent quota contention.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared external resources.
requires-engineering: separate credentials per agent.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate browser-sourced or tool-assisted outputs, and B is an uploader that can act on account data and media. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into incorrect or unwanted social uploads. The profiles do not show verification gates, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated captions, titles, or metadata without verification, errors cascade.
IF A’s browser-derived facts are posted by B, downstream publication can be wrong or misleading.
mitigations: Require human approval before B uploads A-generated content.
Compare A outputs against source media before posting.
Use a checksum or filename match for media selection.
requires-engineering: add a verification step between A and B.
requires-engineering: log provenance for every field B publishes.

E_compliance.rationale: A handles provider auth prompts and session history; B handles account data and media. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so compliance risk is limited to ordinary handling gaps rather than a documented breach pathway. I cite both because the concern is about combined data handling, though no specific mismatch is evidenced.
conditions: IF A’s session history contains regulated data and B uploads it, policy violations may occur.
IF the operator uses the pair for data subject requests without retention controls, compliance gaps emerge.
mitigations: Classify data before moving it from A to B.
Avoid placing regulated data in A’s session history.
Use separate accounts for personal and business uploads.
requires-engineering: document retention and deletion workflows.
requires-engineering: add residency and DPA checks before deployment.
